## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Laplace-type neural operators compute the time axis with a Fourier series, which assumes periodic inputs. They
handle initial conditions only implicitly, and they cannot represent spatial boundaries. We address all three
within one pole-based layer.

1. **Time axis (D1).** On non-periodic inputs the Fourier path costs 1e-4 to 1e-3 relative error from periodicity
   alone, about 100× more than an exact first-order-hold (FOH) recursion on ramps and smooth signals. The FOH
   recursion is causal, O(n) and window-independent, and became the default time axis of project A.
2. **Initial conditions (D2).**
   - Linear systems: a free-response term that shares the poles with the forced response adds one coefficient
     function γ(k). It is recovered to 1e-5, and chained windows reproduce the oracle's rollout exactly.
   - Second-order modes with two initial fields: the free-response coefficients are fixed by the poles. A damped
     beam is identified from its displacement alone (c and η within 1e-4), where free polynomial laws are 50–90×
     worse.
   - Deep nonlinear rollout (Burgers, Cahn–Hilliard): the structural gain is modest.
     - Training windows that start from developed states matter more (−15 %; −30 % together with twice the
       windows). Pushforward training and a semigroup penalty did not help.
     - Pole-based models tolerate initial fields on unseen modes but have no edge at larger amplitudes or over 10
       windows. On unseen modes the error is 0.7× the in-distribution error on Burgers (TFNO 3.3×) and 2.2–2.7×
       on Cahn–Hilliard (TFNO 10×).
     - On Cahn–Hilliard a TFNO rolls out 2× better. A decomposition with the true solver shows this is its
       one-window accuracy carried forward: carried errors contract alike for both models. At a matched budget
       the gap is not closed by changing how the initial field enters, the number of poles, or the depth (3 to 6
       layers).
3. **Boundaries (D3).**
   - Boundary values and fluxes enter the modes as forcing channels whose coefficients are laws in k (∝ k for a
     value, constant for a flux). These are recovered at the oracle floor for Dirichlet, Neumann, mixed and
     advective cases.
   - Where an unknown parameter sets the basis itself, it is identifiable when learned as the physical parameter
     and the basis is computed from it. A Robin coefficient is found by a profile, then released (within 0.3 %). A
     variable diffusion coefficient D(x) is recovered to 1e-4 through a differentiable eigenproblem. Learned freely
     with everything else, such parameters collapse or converge slowly.

## Introduction

The Laplace neural operator [@cao2024lno] and its variants [@ha2026lfno] write a system's response as poles and
residues, with the time axis computed by an FFT over the window. Three things that physical data carry fall
outside that setup:

- inputs that do not repeat at the ends of the window (steps, ramps, PRBS);
- non-zero initial states;
- boundaries in space.

Project D asks how to handle each without losing the pole structure that projects A and C rely on. Every
experiment below was pre-registered, and failed predictions are reported as such.

## The time axis (D1) {#sec-d1}

**Oracle comparison.** We computed, without any training, the response of the true pole–residue systems to 100
inputs per family with each time-axis representation. The inputs are defined on a 32× finer grid and seen only at
the samples.

| input family | Fourier (LNO) | Fourier, pad 2× | FOH | Chebyshev 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| step | 1.7–2.8e-3 | 1.6–2.7e-3 | 1.6–2.7e-3 | 7.3e-3–1.1e-2 |
| ramp | 0.7–1.8e-3 | 1.8–2.9e-4 | **1.2–2.8e-6** | 1.0–1.6e-4 |
| PRBS | 0.9–1.0e-2 | 0.9–1.0e-2 | 0.9–1.0e-2 | 2.9–4.5e-2 |
| smooth, mismatched ends | 4.1–6.7e-4 | 3.0–4.9e-4 | 5.9–7.5e-6 | **1.7–2.2e-8** |
| periodic (control) | 2.9–4.5e-6 | 2.9–4.4e-4 | 1.8–4.0e-5 | **0.5–1.2e-7** |

: Median relative L2 error of the representation alone (systems p2, p4, p6 of project C). {#tbl-d1}

- The Fourier path's error on non-periodic inputs is 10–100× its error on the periodic control. It is spread over
  the whole window rather than concentrated at the ends, and it falls only as $n^{-1}$.
- On steps and PRBS every path is limited by the sampling: a jump between samples cannot be located.
- A global Chebyshev fit is the best representation on smooth inputs. It is numerically unusable at high degree
  (errors up to 1e7 at degree 256) and poor at discontinuities.
- **Trained layers** (E2 recipe, fine-grid truth): the Fourier and FOH layers reach the same test error, the
  sampling floor (3.7e-3 against 3.4e-3). They recover the complex poles in every run and the fast real pole −2 in
  6 of 8 and 4 of 8 runs. The FOH layer's large advantage in (C) E4 came from a model-class match with data that
  had a first-order hold.

**Decision** (user, 2026-11-18): the FOH exponential-integrator recursion is the default time axis, with piecewise
Chebyshev as an option for smooth inputs. It is never worse than Fourier except on periodic inputs, and it is causal,
O(n), and independent of the window length. Project A's time extrapolation and Δt transfer rest on that
independence.

## Initial conditions and rollout (D2) {#sec-d2}

For a pole-based layer, a non-zero initial field u₀ adds the free response

$$\hat u(k,t) \mathrel{+}= \hat u_0(k)\sum_n \gamma_n(k)\, e^{\mu_n(k)\,t},$$

which shares the poles $\mu_n(k)$ with the forced response. Only $\gamma_n(k)$, a polynomial in k² like the
residues, is new. Semigroup consistency is then structural: the last field of one window is the next window's
initial field. A unit test checks that two chained windows reproduce the exact solution to 1e-9.

### Linear systems: exact chaining

**Periodic ADR.** Each window has a random initial field (modes 1–16), the forcing is at half amplitude, and
T = 5. We compare the layer with the initial-condition path (`ic`) and a layer that sees only the forcing (`noic`).
Rollout chains 4 windows over [0, 20].

| model | test / oracle | recovered D, v, k_r | max abs(γ − 1) | rollout / oracle rollout |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| with IC path | **1.00** | 0.0500, 0.5000, 0.2000 | **≤ 1.1e-5** | **1.000–1.001** |
| without IC path | 570–750 | – | – | – |

: Initial-condition path on periodic ADR, 5 data seeds. {#tbl-d2}

- One pre-registered prediction failed: rollout error ≤ 1.5× the single-window test error, which reached 1.73 in
  one seed. The right reference is the oracle's own rollout, which the model matches exactly; the ratio to the
  single-window error reflects the different sample sets through the sampling floor.
### Deep nonlinear rollout

- **Forced Burgers, 4 chained windows.** The deep WPO's initial-state path shares the first
  layer's poles. It gives the lowest rollout error: 0.054, against 0.060 with u₀ as an input channel and 0.061 for
  a TFNO at the same budget. Every model about doubles its error over the 4 windows, so the structural gain is
  real but modest (about 10 %).
- **Training for rollout.** Neither of the plan's remedies helped. Pushforward training (window 2 starts from the
  model's own prediction) raised the mean rollout error from 0.042 to 0.048. The semigroup penalty raised it to 0.045
  and the window error by 14 %. What did help was training on windows that start from developed fields (the state at
  t = 5 of a trajectory), as rollout windows do. This lowered the rollout error from 0.054 to 0.042 with the same
  model.
- **Start states against window count.** A 2 × 2 design separates the two changes. Doubling the windows and making
  half of them developed each lower the rollout error by about 15 %, and the two effects add up (0.060 → 0.042).
  They act differently. More windows lower the window error, and the rollout error follows at a ratio of about 2.5.
  Developed start states raise the error on fresh test windows by 14 % but cut the rollout-to-window ratio to
  about 1.9. Training data for chained windows should therefore be chosen by rollout error, not window error.
- **Generalization and long rollout.** All three models were retrained on developed-start windows.
  - Initial fields on modes never seen in training (9–16): the TFNO's error triples. The two pole-based models do
    not degrade, because their time axis is a pole response in every mode. The IC path is better than the channel
    input (0.72 against 1.08 of the in-distribution error).
  - Initial amplitudes 1–3× beyond training cost every model about 10×, the TFNO least (8.8×).
  - Over 10 windows no model blows up, and per-window errors saturate after window 3. The TFNO has the lowest
    10-window error (0.049 against 0.055), and the IC path's 4-window lead shrinks to 4 %. With good training
    data, the structural rollout advantage is small.
- **A second system: Cahn–Hilliard** (unstable band, saturation at ±1), same protocol.
  - The tolerance of unseen initial modes carries over: TFNO 10.5× its in-distribution error, IC-path WPO 2.4×.
    The IC-path WPO is also lower in absolute error.
  - The rollout finding does not. The TFNO is 2× better in-distribution and over 4 and 10 windows. It is not
    the training budget: at 12000 steps (project A's budget, where the zero-initial-state models were at parity)
    both models improve by 15–30 % and the ratio stays (0.46 against 0.48 over 4 windows); the TFNO's unseen-mode
    ratio grows (13.5 against 2.3).
  - Errors keep growing slowly over 10 windows (1.6–2.1× from window 3 to 10) rather than saturating. A
    decomposition with the true solver run from the models' own states (d2i) shows why. The start error carried
    over is not amplified: the true dynamics contract it to 0.81–0.96 per window, and both models reproduce that
    contraction to within 5 %. Each window adds a local error, and the sum keeps creeping up. (An earlier reading
    here, amplification in the unstable band, does not hold.)
  - The TFNO's rollout edge is its one-window edge carried forward. Its local error is 0.56× the IC path's in every
    window, in the same bands (three quarters at k ≤ 4). Neither model is more stable in rollout.
  - The gap is largest in the response to the initial field. With one input dominant (d2j), the TFNO is 2.0–2.4×
    better when the initial field dominates and 1.4–1.6× when the forcing does. The forcing response is also below
    the zero-initial-state parity of project A.
  - How the initial field enters does not matter (d2k). Four entry points give the same one-window error within
    2 % at a matched budget (0.0255–0.0259): the first-layer IC path, an input channel, separate IC poles, and a
    free response in every layer. The gap is a property of the WPO backbone on this system, not of the IC path.
    Every variant keeps the unseen-mode tolerance (2.4–2.7 against the TFNO's 10.4).
  - Nor is it the temporal expressivity or the depth of the backbone (d2l). Twelve poles at a narrower width are
    worse (0.029). Depth helps with diminishing returns: 3, 4 and 6 layers give 0.032, 0.026 and 0.024. The best
    WPO stays at 2× the TFNO's error; the gap is a property of the two architectures on this system.
  - Nor is it the TFNO's parameter count (d2m). The TFNO had 1.81× the WPO's real parameters (its complex
    weights were counted once). At the WPO's real budget it gives 0.014 against 0.013, 1.8× better than the WPO,
    and its unseen-mode ratio is 13.
### Two initial fields

- **A damped beam.** u_tt = −c²u_xxxx + η u_xxt + f, observed through its displacement, with
  random initial displacement and velocity. For a second-order mode, the free-response coefficients are fixed by
  the poles: (v₀ − μ₂u₀)/(μ₁ − μ₂) and (μ₁u₀ − v₀)/(μ₁ − μ₂), with no free γ. They and the forcing residues
  scale as 1/k², which a polynomial cannot express.
  - With the coefficients written this way (8 reals in all), the layer is at the oracle in every seed, with c and
    η within 1e-4. Four chained windows reproduce the oracle's rollout (0.997–1.001×). The velocity passed between
    windows comes from the model's own modal states, since only u is observed.
  - Free polynomial laws in their place are 50–90× worse, and withholding v₀ gives ~100×.

## Boundaries in space {#sec-bc}

A periodic layer cannot represent boundaries. On [0, L] with Dirichlet values a(t), b(t), the sine transform
diagonalizes diffusion, and the boundary values enter mode m as a forcing:

$$\frac{d\hat u_m}{dt} = \lambda(k_m)\,\hat u_m + \hat f_m(t) + c(k_m)\,\big(a(t) - (-1)^m b(t)\big),\qquad c(k) = \frac{2Dk}{L}.$$

The model is the wavenumber pole layer on sine modes plus a boundary channel $c(k) = c_1k + c_3k^3$ that shares the
poles.

| model | test / oracle | D̂ (0.02) | ĉ₁ (0.04) |
|---|---|---|---|
| sine modes + boundary channel | **1.00–1.04** | **0.01992–0.02007** | **0.03995–0.04001** |
| sine modes, no boundary channel | 82–104 | – | – |
| periodic layer | 84–105 | – | – |

: Diffusion on [0, 1] with time-varying Dirichlet values, 63 interior points, 5 data seeds. {#tbl-bc}

- The truth is the 63-mode sine-Galerkin solution. A finite-difference truth was dropped before any fit: its
  discrete eigenvalues are not polynomial over all modes, so a D-recovery test would have tested the
  discretization.
- **Other boundary types.** With a free cubic law per channel, the layer reproduces Dirichlet, Neumann and mixed
  boundaries at the oracle, with D within 1.2 %. Without the channels the error is 79–283× larger. On the modes the
  data excite (m ≤ 8), each learned law is right within about 1 % and has the physical form: ∝ k for a boundary
  value, constant for a boundary flux. Over all 32 modes it is not (up to 60 %), because high modes leave almost no
  trace. The law is identified where it is excited, as for dispersion relations in project A.
- **Advection.** With u_t = −v u_x + D u_xx, the weight w = e^{−αx}u, α = v/(2D), makes the sine modes diagonal
  again. One learned α recovers 2.00 to 0.4 % in every seed. The error is 1.1× the oracle in 4 of 5 seeds (1.4 in
  one), against 15–17× without the weight. D̂ and the offset v²/(4D) are biased by up to 10 %. Refitting on a truth
  without the 1 % time-axis representation floor cuts the in-band pole error from 7–10 % to 0.4–2 %. Recovered
  constants are therefore only as good as the representation floor allows.
### Parameters that set the basis

- **Robin boundaries.** With D u_x + H u = F at one end, the basis is sin(k_m x) with k_m the roots of
  k cos k + h sin k = 0 (h = H/D; h, not β, which here names the residues), so the basis itself is unknown. Built from the true h, the layer is at the
  oracle with D within 0.8 % and the laws within 1.2 %. Learning h jointly with everything else fails in every
  seed: h collapses to the Neumann end and the error is 6–8× the oracle. A profile works instead. Fit the rest at
  each h on a coarse log grid that excludes the truth, then release h from the best point. This recovers
  h within 0.5 % in every seed, at 1.00–1.11× the oracle. Two of the five seeds missed the D and law criteria with
  the pre-registered 300 iterations after the release. Rerun to convergence (a pre-registered stopping rule), every
  seed meets them: h within 0.3 %, D within 0.7 %, laws within 0.7 %, ≤ 1.011× the oracle.
- **A variable coefficient.** For u_t = (D(x)u_x)_x with D varying threefold, the eigenfunctions are not sines.
  Two ways to learn the basis were compared (@tbl-basis).
  - A free orthogonal basis change Q = exp(S − Sᵀ) with one pole per mode (528 reals) needs thousands of
    iterations. With 600 it missed the pre-registered criteria on the weakly excited modes 7–8; run to
    convergence it meets them in every seed. It gives the eigen-decomposition, not D(x).
  - D(x) on six cosines, with the basis and poles from the eigen-decomposition of the Galerkin operator A(d),
    which is linear in d (6 reals), converges in 600 iterations and recovers D(x) to 1e-4. For a D(x) outside the
    span (0.01·3^x), it lands on the best six-cosine approximation (1.07 % against a floor of 1.06 %).
    A line search can step to D(x) < 0, where the poles turn positive. A penalty keeps the fit in the physical
    region (a fix after the first launch, recorded with the results).

| model | reals | test / oracle | recovered | iterations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sine basis, free poles | 32 | 15–27 | – | 600 |
| free orthogonal basis, free poles | 528 | 1.0005–1.0018 | λ₁..₈ within 0.16 %, eigenvectors ≥ 0.99987 | 3300–6600 |
| D(x) on 6 cosines, basis from eigh | 6 | **1.0000–1.0006** | **D(x) within 2.5e-4**, λ₁..₈ within 1.8e-4 | 600 |
| same, D(x) = 0.01·3^x (outside the span) | 6 | 1.08–1.13 | D(x) within 1.08 % (floor 1.06 %) | 600 |

: Variable coefficient D(x) = 0.02 (1 + 0.5 cos πx), Dirichlet, 5 data seeds; the last row is a second system.
The free basis is reported after running to convergence. {#tbl-basis}

- **The pattern.** Parameters that set the basis, rather than the coefficients in it, are best learned as physical
  parameters with the basis computed from them. Where the loss landscape has a flat edge (the Robin coefficient at
  the Neumann end), add an outer search. As free basis entries they either collapse or converge slowly.
### Where it stops

Project A's Danckwerts reactor (a27) is a convective problem with an inlet and an outlet,
  observed only at the outlet. There the modal poles were not identifiable, and a dead time plus lags described the
data best. Boundaries work as a channel when the basis diagonalizes the operator and the field is observed.

## Discussion

**One structure.** Every input enters through the same poles:
- the forcing through the residues β(k);
- the initial state through γ(k), or, for second-order modes, through coefficients the poles fix;
- the boundary values through c(k).

The coefficients are either low-order laws in k, identified where the data excite them, or determined by the poles
and a few physical parameters. In every linear case the layer reached the oracle floor once the right structure was
in place. What makes this possible is an exact, causal time axis that does not assume periodicity (D1).

**What the structure does not buy.** For deep nonlinear rollout the pole structure gives a modest gain on Burgers
(about 10 % over 4 windows with fresh-start training, 4 % with developed-start training) and none over 10 windows.
On Cahn–Hilliard a TFNO rolls out 2× better. That gap is set within one window, not by rollout instability:
- the true dynamics contract a carried error (0.81–0.96 per window), and both models reproduce that contraction;
- the gap survives four ways of feeding the initial field, twice the poles, 3 to 6 layers (best WPO 0.024
  against 0.013), and an equal real parameter budget (TFNO 0.014; d2m).

The choice of training windows matters more than the architecture. The robust structural benefit is extrapolation
in the mode content of the initial field, which every WPO variant kept (2.2–2.7× against the TFNO's 10.4×). In
project A the same physical-k parametrization also lets a 2D model move to a larger domain without retraining.

**Practice.** Two lessons on fitting came out of failed predictions.
- Fixed iteration budgets under-fit the weakly excited modes. Claims about those modes need a fit run to
  convergence, with the stopping rule stated in advance.
- Parameters must be kept in their physical range (β > 0, D(x) > 0). Otherwise a single line-search step can make
  the operator unstable and end the fit.

## Limitations {.unnumbered}

- Deep rollout: two nonlinear systems in 1D (Burgers, Cahn–Hilliard), 3 seeds, two training budgets (6000 and,
  on Cahn–Hilliard, 12000 steps). Architecture variants at one budget (about 60 k parameters); pushforward
  training and the semigroup penalty were tried on Burgers only.
- Boundaries: 1D diffusion with Dirichlet, Neumann, mixed and Robin boundaries, constant-coefficient advection, and
  one variable coefficient in 1D, with truth and model in the same 32-mode space. Variable coefficients in 2D, and
  inverse problems with observation only at the boundary, are not covered (see the Danckwerts case).
- The convergence rule (relative drop < 1e-4 per 300 iterations) reached its cap in 1 of the 20 reported runs.
- Every test error is limited by the sampling floor of steps and PRBS (about 1 %).
